name: Sentrik
title: An overnight exception desk for robot fleets
summary: Keep commercial robots moving when autonomy stalls, without making the engineering team carry the pager.
buyer: Small indoor robot vendors with 20–200 deployed robots and an overnight support burden.
problem: A short autonomy failure can produce a long operational interruption when nobody is available to recover the robot. The buyer needs dependable exception handling, but may not have enough deployments to justify an internal round-the-clock team.
solution: Operate a remote exception desk using approved vendor control tools. Diagnose incidents, perform permitted resets or rerouting, verify recovery, and escalate physical or hardware failures to onsite staff. Start with one platform rather than promising universal integration.
revenue: Test a paid integration fee plus a monthly coverage retainer with included interventions and usage limits. The supplied $99 and $1,000 fleet plans are hypotheses; price only after measuring total operator time and peak incident load.
gap: The proposed wedge is taking responsibility for a defined exception queue with an agreed response time. A dashboard alone is insufficient differentiation; staffed alternatives already exist.
risks: A robot stuck on a physical threshold may need an onsite person. Remote recovery rate is the central assumption.
Correlated incidents can overwhelm a pooled operator even when average utilization is low.
Vendor permissions, local safety controls, command auditing, and escalation procedures must be agreed before intervention.
Cross-customer data rights and transferable failure patterns are unproven.
pilot: Recruit three paying customers using the same indoor robot platform.
Observe the existing overnight incident queue and classify remote versus physical recoveries.
Run a bounded off-hours service with approved runbooks and onsite escalation.
Measure remote resolution rate, operator minutes per incident, response time during bursts, downtime avoided, and renewal intent.
timing: Vendors with growing deployments may need coverage before they can justify a dedicated operations team. Validate that staffing gap in customer interviews rather than relying on a broad robot-market forecast.
sources: OBI: staffed robot monitoring and teleoperation
sourceNote: These sources establish existing support and control capabilities. They do not establish Sentrik’s demand, recovery rate, or unit economics.

name: Permit Desk
title: A permit tracker for small construction teams
summary: Give contractors one place to track permit requirements, submissions, corrections, and inspection dates.
buyer: Small general contractors juggling several projects across neighboring municipalities.
problem: Permit status lives in city portals, email threads, and employee memory. A missing correction or inspection can interrupt the schedule, while the owner has no reliable view across jobs.
solution: A project-based permit workspace with a checklist, submission history, named owner, due dates, and reusable municipality-specific templates. Begin with customer-entered updates rather than promising integrations with every city portal.
revenue: Test a monthly company subscription based on active projects. Offer a paid concierge setup to learn which steps are genuinely repetitive.
gap: Hypothesis: smaller contractors need a lightweight coordination tool rather than a broad construction management suite. Interviews must establish whether their current suite already does the job.
risks: Municipal requirements vary and can change. Templates need a clear maintenance owner.
Small contractors may prefer a spreadsheet and resist another subscription.
Do not represent a checklist as an authoritative determination of legal requirements.
pilot: Interview five contractors and inspect the permit trail for a recent delayed job.
Track ten live projects manually with shared checklists.
Ask customers to pay for the next month before automating portal integrations.
timing: Test with teams adding projects faster than administrative headcount. No verified market-growth claim is required.

name: Renewal Radar
title: Catch software renewals before the notice deadline
summary: Turn contracts and renewal notices into a calendar of decisions, owners, and cancellation deadlines.
buyer: Operations or finance leads at small companies without a procurement team.
problem: An annual contract renews because nobody remembers the notice deadline. The finance team sees the charge only after the opportunity to renegotiate or cancel has passed.
solution: Extract renewal and notice dates from uploaded contracts, require human confirmation, assign a decision owner, and send reminders before the contractual deadline. Start with manual uploads and avoid broad inbox access.
revenue: Test an annual company subscription and an optional one-time contract inventory service. Price against verified avoided renewals rather than the number of reminders sent.
gap: Hypothesis: a focused renewal workflow can serve teams that find full spend-management platforms excessive. Existing procurement tools are a competitive risk.
risks: Incorrect extraction of a notice period can create costly missed deadlines.
Contract documents contain confidential terms and need appropriate access controls.
A calendar may be sufficient for companies with only a few vendors.
pilot: Inventory contracts for three small companies.
Have the buyer verify every extracted notice deadline.
Track actual decisions and savings across one renewal cycle; seek paid renewal.
timing: Look for customers whose contract inventory has outgrown the founder’s memory.

name: Scope Ledger
title: Turn client requests into approved scope changes
summary: Help specialty contractors document extra work before it quietly becomes unpaid work.
buyer: Owners of small electrical, plumbing, or finish-contracting businesses.
problem: Additional work is requested verbally or by text. The team completes it, but the owner later struggles to demonstrate what changed, who approved it, and what it cost.
solution: A phone-friendly record linking a request, photos, estimated labor and materials, client approval, and invoice reference. Preserve the approval trail and export it to the contractor’s existing system.
revenue: Test a per-company subscription with a simple active-job allowance. Avoid taking a percentage of disputed revenue before understanding collection workflows.
gap: Hypothesis: the approval process can be much quicker than the equivalent workflow in a full project management suite.
risks: Customers may refuse formal approval when work is urgent.
Existing construction software may already cover the workflow.
Approval records need to fit the customer’s contract and business process.
pilot: Follow three contractors through recent scope disputes.
Use a simple approval link on twenty real change requests.
Measure approval turnaround, documentation completeness, and paid conversion.
timing: Focus on contractors with repeat extra-work disputes rather than general digital-transformation messaging.

name: Open Slot
title: A cancellation waitlist for independent clinics
summary: Help front-desk teams fill canceled appointments from a consented, preference-aware waitlist.
buyer: Practice managers at independent outpatient clinics.
problem: When appointments cancel, staff call patients one at a time. Patients who want earlier care are difficult to match by availability, appointment type, and provider.
solution: A consented waitlist that stores availability preferences and sends a controlled invitation when an eligible slot opens. Staff confirm booking through the existing scheduling system. Start without storing clinical details.
revenue: Test a monthly per-location fee. The buyer should evaluate filled slots and staff time saved, not just message volume.
gap: Hypothesis: a narrow waitlist product works where existing scheduling systems have weak cancellation workflows. Confirm this before building.
risks: Scheduling vendors may already include suitable waitlist features.
Patient privacy and messaging requirements affect implementation.
Eligibility rules can be more complex than matching an available time.
pilot: Map the cancellation process at three practices.
Run a staff-assisted waitlist with explicit patient consent.
Measure incremental filled slots, staff effort, opt-outs, and booking errors.
timing: Target practices with recurring cancellations and enough demand to maintain a real waitlist.

name: Fieldproof
title: Maintenance evidence that survives the handoff
summary: Give property managers a clear history of completed work, equipment conditions, and follow-up tasks.
buyer: Property managers coordinating small maintenance vendors across multiple buildings.
problem: A vendor says a repair is finished, but photos, asset details, and unresolved issues remain scattered across texts. The next technician starts without useful context.
solution: A work-order evidence link that captures before-and-after photos, equipment identifiers, a completion checklist, and unresolved issues. Export a concise handoff record without forcing technicians into a complex new system.
revenue: Test per-property or per-active-work-order pricing with a portfolio minimum.
gap: Hypothesis: evidence collection can be lighter than adopting a full maintenance management system. Existing property tools are the comparison to beat.
risks: Technicians may see documentation as unpaid extra work.
Photos alone do not establish that a repair was performed correctly.
Property management software may already supply the needed workflow.
pilot: Review twenty completed work orders with two managers.
Run evidence links with one cooperative maintenance vendor.
Measure missing information, repeat visits, and the manager’s willingness to pay.
timing: Look for portfolios where vendor turnover makes maintenance history especially valuable.

name: Return Desk
title: A returns intake desk for small equipment brands
summary: Collect the evidence and troubleshooting steps needed to route warranty claims quickly.
buyer: Small hardware or equipment brands with a growing support queue.
problem: Warranty requests arrive without serial numbers, useful photos, or a clear fault description. Support staff repeatedly ask for the same missing information before they can make a decision.
solution: A branded intake flow plus a staffed triage desk following the brand’s approved troubleshooting and warranty rules. Deliver a complete case to the decision maker; never invent eligibility or promise refunds.
revenue: Test a monthly minimum plus a per-completed-case fee. Separate straightforward intake from skilled technical diagnosis.
gap: Hypothesis: smaller brands will buy a specialized intake service rather than hire another support agent or configure a larger support system.
risks: Product-specific training can consume the margin.
Poor troubleshooting can frustrate customers or cause unsafe use.
Seasonal or batch defects can cause sudden demand spikes.
pilot: Choose one brand and one product line.
Review fifty historical cases and define an approved intake checklist.
Run a paid pilot measuring case completeness, resolution time, escalations, and cost.
timing: Start with a brand that has an established product and repeatable support volume.

name: Grant Trail
title: Post-award reporting for small nonprofits
summary: Keep grant obligations, reporting deadlines, and supporting evidence in one shared place.
buyer: Executive directors or operations leads at small nonprofits with several active grants.
problem: Winning a grant creates reporting commitments that are spread across award letters, spreadsheets, and program staff. Preparing a report becomes a last-minute search for evidence.
solution: A grant obligation register with confirmed deadlines, assigned owners, budget references, and a running collection of program evidence. Begin with manual award-letter review and export reports for staff approval.
revenue: Test an annual subscription based on active grants, with an optional setup service.
gap: Hypothesis: post-award coordination deserves a simpler tool than a large grants or donor management platform.
risks: Small nonprofit budgets may limit willingness to pay.
Each funder’s reporting requirements can be highly specific.
The product must preserve source requirements rather than generate unsupported outcome claims.
pilot: Review award letters and recent reports at three nonprofits.
Track a reporting cycle using a shared obligation register.
Measure preparation time, missed requirements, and paid renewal intent.
timing: Find organizations whose grant portfolio has grown beyond one person’s informal process.

name: Lesson Loop
title: A practice planner for adult music students
summary: Turn a teacher’s lesson notes into a realistic weekly practice routine.
buyer: Adult learners taking regular private music lessons.
problem: Students leave lessons with several things to practice but little guidance on how to fit them into short sessions. By the next lesson, they have repeated familiar pieces and avoided difficult exercises.
solution: Students or teachers enter lesson goals and available practice time. The planner creates short sessions, records what felt difficult, and summarizes questions for the next lesson. Start with user-entered instructions rather than automated performance grading.
revenue: Test a low-cost student subscription or a teacher plan covering invited students.
gap: Hypothesis: continuity between lessons matters more to this segment than a broad library of video instruction.
risks: Students may abandon planning tools as quickly as they abandon practice.
Teachers may not want another administrative task.
A generic checklist or existing practice app may be sufficient.
pilot: Recruit ten adult learners through two teachers.
Run a four-week manual practice planning pilot.
Measure repeat use, practice completion, teacher feedback, and willingness to pay.
timing: Target learners already paying for lessons; motivation and willingness to spend are still hypotheses to test.

name: Care Handoff
title: A shared task handoff for family caregivers
summary: Help families coordinate practical caregiving tasks without losing context in a group chat.
buyer: Families sharing responsibility for an older relative’s everyday support.
problem: Appointments, groceries, transport, and household tasks pass through group messages. People cannot tell what has been handled, what changed, or who is responsible next.
solution: A shared task board and brief handoff log with owners, dates, and confirmed completion. Keep the first version focused on practical coordination rather than medical advice or medication decisions.
revenue: Test a family subscription, while exploring whether a care organization is a better paying customer.
gap: Hypothesis: a focused handoff workflow is useful enough to displace a family group chat and shared calendar.
risks: Consumer willingness to pay may be weak.
Sensitive family information requires careful privacy design.
All participating caregivers must adopt the workflow for it to be useful.
pilot: Interview families about a recent missed handoff.
Run a two-week coordination pilot with five households.
Measure active participation, duplicate work, missed tasks, and willingness to continue paying.
timing: Recruit around a clear coordination transition, such as a new caregiver joining the family routine.
